title: Training neural networks
text:
What this reading is for
A network architecture is only one part of a learning algorithm. Batch size, learning rate, learning-rate schedule, loss function, preprocessing, and model selection all affect the result. This reading uses one channel-like velocity-profile problem to make those choices concrete. It complements Exercise 2, especially its comparisons of normalization, activations, and physical features.
The examples use PyTorch in the course Python environment. No CFD container, additional dataset, or GPU is needed. The supporting files are training_tools.py and training_strategies_experiments.py. They contain the reusable loop and the experiment definitions. The full, recorded comparisons below were executed on a CPU; they are measurements on this prototype, not claims that one strategy is best for every flow problem.
Before inspecting a comparison, predict what might change and why. Then check the prediction against the curves. A more complicated model or training procedure is useful only if the evidence supports it.

title: Training neural networks
text:
One prototype: channel-like velocity profiles
Let \(\eta=y/\delta\) range from the wall to the channel centerline, with \(\delta=0.5\,\mathrm{m}\), \(\nu=10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), and \(Re_b=2\delta\bar U/\nu\). We generate 12 profiles for \(0.1\leq\bar U\leq1.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) on 128 wall-normal cells, graded toward the wall. Define
\[
a=\frac{Re_b^{0.8}}{30},\qquad
g(\eta)=\log\!\left[1+a(2\eta-\eta^2)\right],\qquad
u_x(\eta_i)=\bar U\frac{g(\eta_i)}{\sum_j w_jg(\eta_j)},
\]
where \(w_j\) are normalized cell-width weights and \(\sum_jw_j=1\). The velocity is zero at the wall, its wall-normal derivative vanishes at the centerline, and its discrete volume-weighted mean is \(\bar U\). This is an explicitly constructed smooth profile family, not an OpenFOAM solution, Spalding’s relation, or a validated turbulence model. It supplies a reproducible training problem with a steep near-wall gradient and a Reynolds-number dependence.
We learn \((\eta,Re_b)\mapsto u_x\). Unlike the dimensionless target in Exercise 2, this prototype uses dimensional velocity as the target, so the common evaluation metric is directly an RMSE in m/s. The same loop also works with a dimensionless target if the evaluation metric correctly reverses all its transformations.
 
Eight complete profiles are used for training, two for validation, and two interior profiles for testing. The split is fixed before fitting input and target standardizers. Training targets receive small, fixed Gaussian perturbations with standard deviation \(0.002\bar U\); validation and test targets remain clean. This lets us distinguish a training observation from the known synthetic reference.
The robust-loss comparison later adds approximately 5% deliberately corrupted training targets. The underlying problem, scalers, and validation profiles remain unchanged; the corrupted experiment is identified separately from the main comparisons.
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from training_tools import ProfileMLP, Standardizer, evaluate, fit, make_profile_problem

torch.set_num_threads(1)  # Fixed CPU setting for these small examples.
problem = make_profile_problem()
train_data = problem["datasets"]["train"]
validation_data = problem["datasets"]["validation"]
test_data = problem["datasets"]["test"]
print(len(train_data), len(validation_data), len(test_data))  # 1024, 256, 256
The standardizer stores training means and standard deviations. A constant feature is assigned scale one, rather than divided by zero. Save the scalers, feature definitions, and split identifiers with a trained model. Applying BatchNorm or LayerNorm inside a network does not replace this data preparation.

title: Training neural networks
text:
What one update actually means
For a batch \(\mathcal B\) of size \(B\), the mean squared error for a scalar output is
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathcal B}(\theta)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}
\left[f_\theta(x_i)-y_i\right]^2.
\]
One optimizer update uses the gradient of this batch loss. An epoch visits the training dataset once. With \(N\) training samples, an epoch normally contains \(\lceil N/B\rceil\) updates if the final smaller batch is retained.








Strategy
Samples used per update
Consequence




Full batch
All training samples
One update per epoch; the gradient uses the entire current dataset.


Mini-batch
A subset, for example 64
More updates per epoch; gradients depend on which samples are grouped together.


Single-sample stochastic updates
One
High update frequency and substantial sampling variability; incompatible with ordinary training-mode BatchNorm1d on these feature vectors.



An equal-epoch comparison without early stopping holds data exposure approximately fixed but gives smaller batches more optimizer updates. An equal-update comparison without early stopping holds the number of updates fixed but exposes larger batches to more samples. Neither also fixes runtime. For this reason, we record epochs, actual updates, samples seen, and elapsed time. Sampling noise, parameter initialization, and dropout are different sources of variability.
The displayed experiments use equal weight per cell sample; Exercise 2 asks you to state and justify your weighting choice. A graded mesh therefore puts more loss terms near the wall. Cell-volume weighting would define a different objective and must be applied consistently, rather than introduced only when a result looks unfavorable.

title: Training neural networks
text:
A reusable supervised training loop
The loop accepts a model, data loaders, a loss, an optimizer, and optionally a scheduler and common evaluation metric. It does not know the CFD case structure: split profiles and build features before creating loaders. It never receives a test loader.
The essential sequence is:

Set model.train() and iterate over shuffled training batches.
Clear gradients, compute predictions and loss, backpropagate, and update the parameters.
Evaluate the current model with model.eval() and disabled gradient recording.
Record a common validation metric, update the schedule at its specified frequency, and retain a copy of the best model state, including normalization buffers.
Restore the validation-selected state after the training budget or optional early-stopping criterion is reached.

The actual implementation used for the comparisons is shown below. The complete supporting file also defines evaluate, the standardizer, and the model components.
from copy import deepcopy
from time import perf_counter

def fit(model, train_loader, validation_loader, loss_fn, optimizer, *, epochs=100,
        metric_fn=None, scheduler=None, scheduler_interval='epoch',
        max_updates=None, patience=20, device='cpu'):
    """Return validation-selected state and history; never access test data."""
    if patience is not None and patience < 1:
        raise ValueError('patience must be positive')
    if epochs < 1 or (max_updates is not None and max_updates < 1):
        raise ValueError('Training budgets must be positive')
    if scheduler_interval not in ('epoch', 'update', 'validation'):
        raise ValueError('Unknown scheduler interval')
    plateau = isinstance(scheduler, torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau)
    if scheduler is not None and plateau != (scheduler_interval == 'validation'):
        raise ValueError('ReduceLROnPlateau requires validation stepping')
    model.to(device)
    history, best, best_value, stale, updates, samples = [], None, float('inf'), 0, 0, 0
    start = perf_counter()
    for epoch in range(1, epochs + 1):
        model.train()
        online_sum, online_n, lr_first, lr_last = 0., 0, None, None
        for x, y in train_loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            if len(x) < 2 and any(isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm1d) for m in model.modules()):
                raise ValueError('BatchNorm training requires at least two samples per batch')
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            pred = model(x)
            loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
            if loss.ndim or not torch.isfinite(loss):
                raise FloatingPointError('Loss must be a finite scalar mean')
            loss.backward()
            if any(p.grad is not None and not torch.isfinite(p.grad).all() for p in model.parameters()):
                raise FloatingPointError('Non-finite gradient')
            lr_last = optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr']
            lr_first = lr_last if lr_first is None else lr_first
            optimizer.step()
            updates += 1
            samples += len(x)
            online_sum += len(x) * loss.item()
            online_n += len(x)
            if scheduler is not None and scheduler_interval == 'update':
                scheduler.step()
            if max_updates is not None and updates >= max_updates:
                break
        if not online_n:
            raise ValueError('Empty training loader')
        validation = evaluate(model, validation_loader, loss_fn, metric_fn, device)
        # Fixed-order evaluation makes training and validation curves comparable.
        training = evaluate(model, DataLoader(train_loader.dataset, batch_size=1024),
                            loss_fn, metric_fn, device)
        if scheduler is not None:
            if scheduler_interval == 'validation':
                scheduler.step(validation['metric'])
            elif scheduler_interval == 'epoch':
                scheduler.step()
        improved = validation['metric'] < best_value
        if improved:
            best_value, stale = validation['metric'], 0
            best = {'model': deepcopy(model.state_dict()),
                    'optimizer': deepcopy(optimizer.state_dict()),
                    'scheduler': None if scheduler is None else deepcopy(scheduler.state_dict()),
                    'epoch': epoch, 'updates': updates}
        else:
            stale += 1
        history.append({'epoch': epoch, 'updates': updates, 'samples_seen': samples,
                        'online_loss': online_sum / online_n,
                        'train_loss': training['loss'], 'validation_loss': validation['loss'],
                        'train_metric': training['metric'], 'validation_metric': validation['metric'],
                        'lr_first': lr_first, 'lr_last': lr_last,
                        'seconds': perf_counter() - start})
        if (max_updates is not None and updates >= max_updates) or (patience is not None and stale >= patience):
            break
    model.load_state_dict(best['model'])
    model.eval()
    return {'history': history, 'best': best, 'best_validation_metric': best_value}
loss_fn must return a scalar mean over equally weighted samples, with a fixed number of target components for regression. The code aggregates evaluation batches using their sample counts. Averaging the means of unequal-sized batches without those counts would give the small final batch too much weight. The online loss is accumulated while parameters change; the separately recorded training metric is evaluated with the final state of that epoch, in evaluation mode, like the validation metric.
The generic interface handles regression tensors (N, n_features) and (N, n_targets). It also handles classification if the network returns class logits and the caller uses CrossEntropyLoss with integer targets (N,) and a suitable common metric. It is not a complete PINN or reinforcement-learning trainer: those require additional residuals, sampling, or trajectory handling. If you introduce sample or class weights, use aggregation matching that weighted objective rather than assuming the present sample-count average is sufficient.

Minimal use on the prototype
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
torch.manual_seed(11)
train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_data, batch_size=64, shuffle=True,
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(1011),
)
validation_loader = DataLoader(validation_data, batch_size=1024)
model = ProfileMLP(width=32, depth=3, activation="silu").to(device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.003)
velocity_scale = problem["y_scaler"].scale.to(device)

def dimensional_mse(prediction, target):
    return ((prediction - target) * velocity_scale).square().mean()

result = fit(
    model, train_loader, validation_loader, nn.MSELoss(), optimizer,
    epochs=240, metric_fn=dimensional_mse, device=device,
)
validation_rmse = result["best_validation_metric"] ** 0.5
This selects a CUDA GPU when available and otherwise uses the CPU. The model is moved before constructing its optimizer, and the metric scale is placed on the same device. The datasets stay in CPU memory; fit transfers each training and validation batch to device. The recorded comparisons here were executed on CPU.
result["best"] includes model, optimizer, and scheduler states at the selected epoch. For inference, save the model state, architecture settings, and scalers. Exact continuation of a shuffled stochastic run additionally requires random-generator/sampler state and a defined continuation point; the example does not implement an exact restart facility. A checkpoint selected by validation error is also distinct from the last training checkpoint.

title: Training neural networks
section: Controlled comparisons and how to read them
text:
Controlled comparisons and how to read them
The main reference model has three hidden layers of width 32 with SiLU activations, an affine output, batch size 64, Adam with learning rate 0.003, and MSE loss. There is no weight decay. The maximum budget is 240 epochs, with early-stopping patience 20. Each setting is repeated with seeds 11, 22, and 33. Data generation and the profile split are fixed; seed changes affect initialization, shuffling, and stochastic layers.
A shared seed controls a random-number stream; it does not make networks with different parameter layouts start from identical functions. Parameter counts are recorded with the results. These are modest, controlled comparisons with fixed settings, not equally exhaustive tuning of every method.
Curves show clean-validation dimensional RMSE: the solid line is the mean over seeds with recorded evaluations at that point, and the shading spans their minimum and maximum. Curves end when all seeds have stopped; stopped histories are not extended. Values are linearly interpolated between recorded evaluations where needed. It is training-run variation, not a predictive confidence interval. Checkpoints are selected by the common validation metric, not by whichever training loss happens to be numerically smallest. The test profiles are used only after selecting a clean-data configuration by its mean best validation MSE across seeds.

Batch size: compare epochs and updates
 
The two axes tell different stories: one counts optimizer updates, the other counts cumulative data exposure in epoch equivalents. Before early stopping, the maximum is 240 updates for full-batch training and 15,360 for batch size 16. If it learns more slowly per epoch, first separate the number of updates from the quality of each gradient estimate. Small batches can make the path noisier; they do not guarantee better generalization or faster execution.
Validation is recorded at epoch boundaries (including a final partial epoch), so runs have different evaluation spacing on the update axis. Under a fixed-update budget, the number of checkpoint-selection opportunities also differs. Early stopping can also change the realized budget. The results table records actual update ranges and final validation errors separately from the best-checkpoint errors; this is a common maximum-budget comparison, not a guarantee of equal work.
A second comparison allows each run up to 1,600 optimizer updates, subject to the same early-stopping rule. Larger batches then see more training samples, and the number of completed epochs differs:
 
The best-checkpoint ranking changes between the epoch-capped and update-capped comparisons. Early stopping also means that actual update counts can differ within each group. The latter also sees more samples per update. The change in ranking shows why the comparison budget must be stated.


Learning rate: step length matters
The learning rate controls the scale of a parameter update. Too small a rate may leave a model under-trained within the available budget; too large a rate can cause oscillations or divergence. Adam adapts updates per parameter but still needs a sensible global learning rate. A larger network, a different activation, target scaling, and batch size can all change which rate works well.
 
All three rates use the same architecture and 240-epoch budget. A finite but poor curve is a valid outcome, not a reason to remove that run. The helper explicitly raises on non-finite losses or gradients. If a setting diverges, record the failure and change it as a new experiment.


Learning-rate schedules








Schedule
Change rule in this example
When step is called

No scheduler

Schedulers are stepped after the corresponding optimizer work, not before the first optimizer update. ReduceLROnPlateau consumes the validation metric; StepLR and CosineAnnealingLR do not. A per-epoch schedule cannot be compared with a per-update schedule merely by giving their counters the same integer. The PyTorch optimizer documentation describes these interfaces and ordering.
 
 
With these budgets and stopping rules, plateau decay has lower mean best validation error than the constant-rate reference; step and cosine decay give different outcomes. These observations concern the stated rates and budgets; they do not establish a general ranking of schedules.
A decreasing rate can help refine a fit, but reducing it before useful progress has been made can also freeze a poor solution. Plateau scheduling and early stopping serve different purposes: one changes update sizes, while the other terminates training. The default is patience=20: training stops after 20 consecutive validation evaluations without a new best metric. Set patience=None to disable early stopping. Each run has a maximum of 240 epochs (or 1,600 updates in the update-budget comparison), and restores its best validation checkpoint. Scheduler patience is separate and controls learning-rate reductions.
When the epoch cap is reached: if early stopping has not triggered, optimization may still benefit from more epochs, especially if validation error continues to decrease. This is a reason to try a larger budget, not a guarantee of improved generalization. The maximum epoch budget is deliberately kept modest in this educational notebook so the comparisons remain practical to run.


Architecture variants
The model factory makes the modifications explicit. depth=3 means one input-to-hidden layer followed by two hidden blocks, then the affine output.
class HiddenBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width, normalization, activation, dropout, residual):
        super().__init__()
        norm = {'none': nn.Identity, 'layer': lambda: nn.LayerNorm(width),
                'batch': lambda: nn.BatchNorm1d(width)}[normalization]
        self.branch = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(width, width), norm(), activation(),
                                    nn.Dropout(dropout))
        self.residual = residual

    def forward(self, x):
        out = self.branch(x)
        return x + out if self.residual else out

class ProfileMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in=2, n_out=1, width=32, depth=3, normalization='none',
                 residual=False, concatenate=False, dropout=0., activation='silu'):
        super().__init__()
        if depth < 1:
            raise ValueError('depth must be positive')
        act = {'tanh': nn.Tanh, 'relu': nn.ReLU, 'silu': nn.SiLU}[activation]
        self.input = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n_in, width), act())
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([
            HiddenBlock(width, normalization, act, dropout, residual)
            for _ in range(depth - 1)
        ])
        self.concatenate = concatenate
        self.output = nn.Linear(width + (n_in if concatenate else 0), n_out)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.input(x)
        for block in self.blocks:
            h = block(h)
        if self.concatenate:
            h = torch.cat((h, x), dim=-1)
        return self.output(h)








Variant
What changes
What to watch




Plain MLP
Repeated affine maps and activations
A useful reference before adding components.


LayerNorm
Normalize hidden features within each sample, with learned scale and offset
No batch statistics; can still change how scalar information is represented.


BatchNorm
Normalize hidden features using training-batch statistics and retain running statistics for evaluation
Batch composition, small batches, and training/evaluation modes matter.


Additive residual connection
Pass \(h+F(h)\) to the next block
Shapes must match; the implemented width is constant.


Concatenated skip connection
Pass the original input to the output layer alongside the final hidden representation
Unlike addition, concatenation increases the next layer’s input dimension.


Dropout
Randomly zero hidden activations during training, with the module’s scale compensation
Evaluation disables dropout; regularization can underfit a small smooth dataset.



BatchNorm1d uses batch statistics during training and, with the default configuration used here, running statistics in evaluation. LayerNorm uses statistics within each input in both modes. Their behavior is therefore not interchangeable. The helper rejects a singleton training batch when BatchNorm is present; choose a compatible batch partition instead of silently losing samples.
 
The residual variant has the same trainable parameter count as the plain model in this implementation; normalization and concatenated-input variants add parameters. Dropout adds no trainable parameters but changes the training process. None is guaranteed to improve this small regression problem. A fair follow-up would give each architecture a comparable validation-based tuning budget.
Activation functions also matter. The following holds width, depth, normalization, optimizer, and budget fixed while replacing SiLU with tanh or ReLU:
 


Loss functions: what errors should the model emphasize?
For a scalar residual \(r=\hat y-y\), MSE uses \(r^2\), MAE uses \(|r|\), and Huber loss uses
\[
\ell_\delta(r)=
\begin{cases}
\frac12r^2,& |r|\leq\delta,\\
\delta\left(|r|-\frac12\delta\right),& |r|>\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
MSE gives a growing gradient to large residuals. MAE gives a gradient with constant magnitude away from zero. Huber combines a quadratic center with linear tails; it can reduce the influence of large corrupted targets while retaining a smooth central region. These objectives can favor different conditional statistics and should be chosen to match the problem, rather than only to obtain a smaller displayed training number. PyTorch HuberLoss defines the threshold convention used here.
For this comparison, all three losses see the same corrupted training targets: every twentieth scaled target receives an offset of 3. The Huber threshold is 0.2 in standardized target units, corresponding to \(0.2s_y\) m/s, where \(s_y\) is the training target standard deviation. Scalers remain fixed across this controlled corruption experiment. A reference MSE run without outliers appears as a separate clean-data control in the figure.
 
The corrupted-target MSE runs have substantially higher validation error than the MAE and Huber runs here. The clean MSE control separates the effect of target corruption from changing the loss.
The vertical axis is the same clean-validation RMSE in m/s for every loss. Comparing raw MAE, MSE, and Huber values would mix different objectives and scales. Robust losses do not repair physically inconsistent labels, poor mesh resolution, or an unrepresentative dataset. Here the corruption is known because we introduced it; real data require independent quality checks.

Combining training strategies
A strategy that helps on its own need not help in combination: normalization changes the activations seen by later layers, and the schedule changes the optimization path. This comparison tests a small factorial set: LayerNorm with SiLU, tanh, or ReLU, each with constant learning rate 0.003 or validation-based plateau decay. LayerNorm was the strongest individual architecture in the preceding comparison; all three activations are retained rather than assuming the individually best activation remains best with normalization.
All six combinations use the same training-only scalers, profile split, MSE objective, batch size 64, width 32, three hidden layers, a maximum of 240 epochs, and seeds 11, 22, and 33. Plateau decay uses factor 0.5, patience 10, and minimum learning rate 0.00001. The LayerNorm–SiLU–constant configuration reuses the architecture reference. title: Training neural networks
section: Final run: let early stopping decide
text:
Final run: let early stopping decide
The selected LayerNorm + SiLU + validation-based plateau schedule is trained with a generous 50,000-epoch maximum and early-stopping patience 20. title: Introduction to machine learning
Introduction to machine learning
text:
Part 1 — Theory
Answer the questions before starting the practical project. Justify your choices rather than listing definitions. You will revisit your answers using your own simulation and training results.

Task 1 — Define the learning problem
We want to predict a fully developed mean streamwise velocity profile in a turbulent channel for different prescribed bulk velocities. The geometry, fluid viscosity, mesh, and turbulence model are initially fixed.

State the experience/data, task, and performance measure in Mitchell’s definition of machine learning for this problem.
Propose inputs and outputs for a model that predicts the velocity at one wall-normal location. Distinguish a feature, a feature value, a target, one point sample, and one complete simulation case.
Is this regression, classification, or unsupervised learning? Explain whether a fixed, trained multilayer perceptron is parametric or non-parametric and deterministic or probabilistic.
Propose a simple baseline, an intended use, and measurable acceptance criteria. What evidence would be needed to claim that the surrogate saves time after accounting for data generation and training?



Task 2 — Design the simulation campaign
Assume a budget of 16 simulations and a bulk-velocity range of \(0.1\leq\bar{U}\leq1.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Sketch a regular grid, independent uniform random sampling, and Latin hypercube sampling in this one-dimensional interval. What does stratification guarantee, and what does it leave random?
How does the cost of a regular grid change if viscosity and channel height also vary, with 16 levels per parameter? Contrast this with a fixed total budget of 16 cases.
Explain why sampling uniformly in a dimensional parameter need not produce uniform coverage in a transformed feature space, such as \(\log Re\).
Propose an adaptive sampling criterion based on validation errors. Why should the untouched test set not guide the next sample locations?
List checks required before treating a final CFD field as a reference label. Can a small training loss compensate for unconverged or poorly resolved reference simulations?



Task 3 — Split and normalize without leakage
Each simulation produces 200 closely related wall-normal samples.

Compare randomly splitting all point samples with splitting entire simulations. Which evaluates generalization to an unseen Reynolds number more directly?
Define interpolation and extrapolation tests for this dataset. Sketch a split with training cases on both sides of an unseen interior test case.
Write the min–max and standardization formulas. Which subset supplies their statistics? Explain how to transform an unseen value outside the training range and how to handle a constant feature.
Explain why normalizing all data before splitting leaks information. Why is repeatedly selecting architectures using test errors also leakage?
State what must be saved alongside trained network weights so that a new input receives exactly the same preprocessing and output transformation.



Task 4 — Use physical knowledge
Let \(\delta\) be the channel half-height, \(\nu\) the kinematic viscosity, \(y\) the wall distance, and \(u_\tau=\sqrt{|\tau_w|/\rho}\) the friction velocity. Define
\[
Re_b=\frac{2\delta\bar{U}}{\nu},\qquad
u^+=\frac{u_x}{u_\tau},\qquad
y^+=\frac{yu_\tau}{\nu}.
\]
Here \(u^+\) denotes dimensionless velocity; it is distinct from the kinematic viscosity \(\nu\).

Compare the mappings \((y,\bar{U})\mapsto u_x\), \((y/\delta,Re_b)\mapsto u_x/\bar{U}\), and \(\log(y^+)\mapsto u^+\). What assumptions allow the final mapping to omit an explicit Reynolds-number input?
Why is \(\log(y^+)\) undefined at the wall? Which wall-normal region might fail to collapse onto a universal curve even when near-wall scaling works well?
Suppose \(u_\tau\) is extracted from a completed CFD solution. Is it available when the surrogate is used to avoid that simulation? Propose an alternative and explain the additional error it introduces.
Would permutation importance or a correlation heatmap prove that a feature is physically causal? Discuss correlated inputs and availability during deployment.



Task 5 — Train and evaluate

For scalar regression, write the mean squared error and derive the gradient-descent update for network parameters. Distinguish parameters from architecture and optimizer hyperparameters.
Explain why an MLP with only affine layers cannot represent an arbitrary nonlinear profile, regardless of its depth.
Propose a fair comparison of two architectures using validation data and multiple random seeds. Distinguish training variability from predictive uncertainty.
Choose plots that reveal near-wall errors, errors at different Reynolds numbers, and variation between runs. Explain what an aggregate error alone can conceal.
Explain why agreement with a RANS dataset establishes an approximation of that dataset, rather than experimental validation of the physical flow.

title: Introduction to machine learning
text:
Part 2 — Practical project

Preparation and working folders
Complete Exercise 1 — System setup, including the OpenFOAM and Basilisk container setup. Use the Ubuntu course environment on native Linux, WSL, or VirtualBox. Run ParaView outside the containers. Keep your scripts and results in exercises; keep the supplied cases in test_cases unchanged.
Start a Bash terminal in the repository root:
source ml-cfd/bin/activate
source setup-env
mkdir -p exercises
Repeat the environment activation and source setup-env in each new terminal. The latter selects the course OpenFOAM.com v2606 image. The Allrun scripts use the repository’s RunFunctions helpers to execute applications and write logs. Existing logs can cause an application to be skipped on a repeated run. Use a fresh working copy for a new experiment; preserve results before using a case’s Allclean script, which deletes generated output.
The commands below assume the named destination folders do not already exist. If you worked with these cases before, choose new folder names and adjust the subsequent paths. Record image names, settings, runtime, and any failures. Runtime depends on the machine, mesh, and output frequency; measure a pilot run before committing to a parameter study.


Task 6 — OpenFOAM: flow past a cylinder

Inspect and execute the case
From the repository root:
cp -r test_cases/cylinder2D exercises/cylinder2D
cd exercises/cylinder2D
Inspect Allrun, system, constant, and 0.org before running:

Identify the solver, viscosity, turbulence treatment, mesh generation utility, and required initial fields.
Read the inlet profile and cylinder diameter. Compute Reynolds numbers using both the maximum and the mean inlet speed. State the convention whenever you report \(Re\).
Determine the number of MPI ranks from system/decomposeParDict; compare it with the resources available to you. If you change the decomposition, explain how its settings remain consistent.
Identify time-step size, end time, write interval, pressure solver, and momentum-convection discretization.
Inspect the forceCoeffs configuration: reference speed, reference area, reference length, and lift/drag directions. Why must these be known when comparing coefficients?

Execute the case and check the mesh:
./Allrun
source "$ML_CFD_BASE/RunFunctions"
runApplication checkMesh
Inspect log.blockMesh, log.checkMesh, and the solver log (log.pimpleFoam). Check for errors, achieved final time, Courant numbers, residuals, continuity errors, and execution time. Explain what the processor* directories contain. A script reaching its last line is not sufficient evidence that every application succeeded.


Visualize fields and force histories
paraview post.foam
Select Decomposed Case before applying the OpenFOAM reader. Inspect the mesh, pressure, velocity magnitude, and vortex shedding. If using a reconstructed case instead, use the corresponding reconstructed-case reader setting. The reconstruction and shared-folder route is described in Exercise 1.
Locate the force output:
find postProcessing -type f -name 'coefficient.dat'
Create your own Python script to load and plot drag and lift coefficients over time. Inspect the header before choosing columns and separators: column positions must follow the actual file, rather than an assumed layout. Label axes and units, identify an initial transient, and state the time interval used for any averages or fluctuation measures. Compare the reference speed in the coefficient definition with your Reynolds-number convention.
Keep: a case-settings summary, mesh/log checks, one flow-field image, and force-history plots. Explain which parts could provide inputs, targets, or quality checks for a later ML problem.



Task 7 — Basilisk: an axisymmetric rising bubble

Compile the solver
Return to the repository root. The solver source is bubble_axis_symmetric.c; the supplied Makefile builds the executable bubble using the Basilisk compiler qcc and MPI.
cd "$ML_CFD_BASE"
cp -r test_cases/basilisk_solver exercises/basilisk_solver
apptainer shell "$ML_CFD_BASE/basilisk.sif"
Inside the container, run:
cd exercises/basilisk_solver
make > log.make 2>&1
cat log.make
Check that compilation succeeded and the bubble executable exists. Inspect the includes, initial condition, acceleration, adaptive refinement, and output events in the source. Contrast this compiled, event-based setup with OpenFOAM’s case dictionaries.


Execute and inspect the simulation
Still inside the container:
mkdir run
cd run
mpirun -np 2 ../bubble 14 10 115 134 > log.solver 2>&1
exit
The arguments are maximum adaptive refinement level, end time, Bond/Eötvös number, and Galilei number. Use an MPI rank count supported by your machine. For a first execution check, you may use a shorter integer end time in a separate pilot directory; this does not replace the full physical run. The source parses end time as an integer and separately sets an initial refinement level, so lowering the maximum adaptive level alone does not necessarily make initialization inexpensive.
Inspect the numerical rows of log.solver. The source writes time, gas-volume measure, three center-of-mass coordinates, three center-of-mass velocity components, and interface area. Identify the rising direction from the source and plot rise speed over time. Assess volume drift and whether the late-time behavior appears settled. Distinguish the axisymmetric calculation from a fully three-dimensional bubble-path simulation.
From an Ubuntu terminal outside the container:
cd "$ML_CFD_BASE/exercises/basilisk_solver/run/vtu"
paraview
Open the bubble_*.pvtu time series and the plic_*.pvtu interface series. Inspect adaptive cell sizes and volume fraction \(f\): this solver uses \(f=0\) in gas and \(f=1\) in liquid. Visualize the interface and velocity. To examine the wake in a translating frame, subtract the measured instantaneous rise velocity from the corresponding velocity component; do not assume a fixed rise speed from an earlier run.
Keep: compilation/execution checks, a rise-speed history, a volume-conservation diagnostic, and a labeled flow/interface image. Explain why changing numerical resolution can change the labels generated by a simulation.



Task 8 — Boundary-layer regression: generate channel profiles
The case in boundary_layer_1D computes a wall-normal profile in a fully developed turbulent plane channel: a no-slip lower wall and symmetry at the half-height, periodic streamwise boundaries, and a mean-velocity forcing term. It is not a spatially developing flat-plate boundary layer.

Inspect the base case and vary one input manually
From the repository root:
cd "$ML_CFD_BASE"
cp -r test_cases/boundary_layer_1D exercises/boundary_layer_1D
cd exercises/boundary_layer_1D
bash ./Allrun
source "$ML_CFD_BASE/RunFunctions"
runApplication checkMesh
The base mesh has 200 wall-normal cells with grading toward the wall. Verify this using the mesh dictionary and mesh check. Read the velocity boundary conditions, system/fvOptions, viscosity, and turbulence model. Identify the prescribed bulk speed \(\bar{U}\) and explain how meanVelocityForce drives the flow. Here \(\delta=0.5\,\mathrm{m}\), \(\nu=10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), and \(Re_b=2\delta\bar{U}/\nu\).
Inspect the final velocity profile in ParaView. Check the solver log and late-time profile changes before accepting it as a reference. purgeWrite retains only a limited number of output times; if more snapshots are needed to assess stationarity, change that setting in your working copy before running.
Make a second fresh copy of the supplied base case with a different destination name. Double \(\bar{U}\) in system/fvOptions, halve deltaT, and halve endTime to preserve \(\tilde{t}=t\bar{U}/(2\delta)\). Run it and compare the profiles. Explain why equal dimensionless run duration does not itself prove convergence.


Automate a small parameter study
cd "$ML_CFD_BASE"
cp test_cases/parameter_variation_1d.py exercises/parameter_variation_1d.py
Inspect your copy before execution. It samples bulk velocity using Latin hypercube sampling, modifies Ubar, deltaT, and endTime, creates Ub_* case folders under exercises/boundary_layer_1D_variation, and launches serial simulations using a worker pool.

Start with two pilot cases and one worker, using --samples 2 --workers 1. Select 10–30 cases for the full study. The script defaults to 16 cases, up to two workers (limited by available CPUs), and seed 2026; change the seed with --seed and record it.
Choose the worker count based on your actual CPU and memory allocation. Each OpenFOAM case runs serially. Keep the total workload within that allocation.
Inspect the generated dictionaries. The script scales end time and time step inversely with speed, records sampled speeds in study.json, and retains three written time directories for late-time comparisons. Verify the configured speeds and dimensionless duration.
Use a new output directory for each study. The script refuses to reuse an existing directory, preventing results from different configurations from being mixed. Select another destination with --output.
Check every solver log, final time, and profile. The script checks process failures and whether the solver reached its configured end time; these checks do not establish convergence. Compare the last saved profiles and extend the run if they still change appreciably.

From the repository root, run a pilot:
source ml-cfd/bin/activate
source setup-env
python exercises/parameter_variation_1d.py --samples 2 --workers 1 --output exercises/channel_pilot
After checking the pilot, run the full study in a separate, new directory:
python exercises/parameter_variation_1d.py --samples 16 --workers 2


Assemble and inspect the dataset
Write a script in exercises using pathlib, PyTorch, Matplotlib, and flowtorch.data.FOAMDataloader. The following is a starting pattern for reading one serial case:
from pathlib import Path
from flowtorch.data import FOAMDataloader

case = Path("exercises/boundary_layer_1D")  # run Python from the repository root
loader = FOAMDataloader(str(case))
y = loader.vertices[:, 1]
time = loader.write_times[-1]
u_x = loader.load_snapshot("U", time)[:, 0]
order = y.argsort()
y, u_x = y[order], u_x[order]
Extend this to every successful Ub_* case. Check the solver end time and the selected snapshot time: the solver can finish between scheduled field writes. Record both, and check that the selected snapshot is suitable for your analysis. Check that coordinates are consistent across cases, values are finite, and units and shapes are correct. Sort each profile by wall distance and cases by their configured bulk velocity. Use a matrix with shape (number of cells, number of cases) for the profiles, plus a case table containing speed, Reynolds number, final time, and quality checks. Plot profiles with a color or legend encoding \(Re_b\).
Because the wall-normal mesh is graded, a plain arithmetic mean over cells does not represent the bulk speed. Use cell-volume weighting when checking the computed mean velocity. Likewise, state whether your regression metric weights cell samples equally or approximates a spatial integral.



Task 9 — Train a direct regression model
Implement the workflow in your own script; use the lecture’s definitions and the optional Python refresher as needed. The optional reading Training neural networks provides a reusable supervised training loop and controlled comparisons of batch sizes, learning rates, schedules, architectures, and losses.

Define the pointwise mapping \((y/\delta,Re_b)\mapsto u_x/\bar{U}\). Write down input and target units and tensor shapes: features (N, 2) and targets (N, 1) for a scalar-output MLP.
Split entire simulation profiles into training, validation, and test subsets before fitting scalers. Keep the test case IDs fixed. Include unseen interior Reynolds numbers for interpolation; label a separate extrapolation evaluation if you reserve cases outside the training range.
Fit normalization statistics using training data only. Save the split and scalers. Check zero-variance features and confirm the transformation can be inverted.

Compare training with and without normalization. Train the direct model twice: first with the feature and target values from step 1 unchanged, and then with statistical normalization of both features and targets. The dimensionless definitions in step 1 remain the same in both runs; only the statistical scaling changes. Fit scaling statistics using training profiles only. For this comparison, keep the network architecture, initialization seed, case split, optimizer, learning rate, and training budget identical. Repeat the paired comparison for several seeds.
Plot training and validation histories, compare convergence and stability, and evaluate dimensional velocity errors after undoing all scaling. Raw losses in different target scales are not directly comparable; also track the same dimensional error measure for both runs. Explain any differences using the feature ranges, activation functions, and gradient-based optimization. If you tune the learning rate separately afterward, report that as an additional comparison and give both approaches the same tuning budget.

Establish a piecewise linear baseline using only training profiles on the common wall-normal grid. At each wall distance, interpolate linearly in bulk velocity between the two bracketing training profiles. Below or above the training interval, extend the segment defined by the lowest or highest two training velocities, respectively. Use dimensional velocity profiles for this calculation. Do not clamp predictions to an endpoint profile: numpy.interp does this by default outside its input range, so implement the linear extension explicitly. The baseline reproduces its training profiles exactly; zero training error is therefore not evidence of generalization.
Train a small PyTorch MLP with nonlinear hidden activations and a scalar output. Use an MSE loss, monitor training and validation losses, and retain the checkpoint selected by validation performance. State the sample weighting: explain how much each cell sample contributes to the loss. Equal weights give every sample the same influence and emphasize the densely sampled near-wall region on this graded mesh. Cell-volume weights instead approximate a spatially averaged error. State which choice you use for training and evaluation.
Test different hidden-layer activation functions, for example tanh, ReLU, and SiLU. First keep layer count, width, normalization, optimizer, learning rate, case split, and training budget fixed so that you can isolate the effect of the activation function. Repeat with several initialization seeds. Compare training and validation histories, convergence, and dimensional prediction errors. Then vary hidden-layer count and width with a modest, recorded budget. Use validation data for selecting the activation and architecture; reserve the test set for evaluating the selected procedure.
Undo target normalization and dimensional scaling before comparing dimensional predictions. Plot predicted and reference profiles, residuals versus wall distance, and errors versus Reynolds number. Report RMSE and maximum absolute error with units, and variation between runs.

Discuss near-wall and centerline behavior as well as aggregate accuracy. If a good average score conceals a poor profile in part of the domain, revisit the validation analysis rather than tuning against the test set.


Task 10 — Compare physical feature transformations

Wall scaling and Spalding’s relation
Estimate friction velocity for each reference case. One option is
\[
u_\tau=\sqrt{\nu\left|\frac{\partial u_x}{\partial y}\right|_w},
\]
using the no-slip wall and resolved near-wall gradient. Explain how you estimate that gradient, assess sensitivity to the near-wall discretization, and distinguish this estimate from a solver-reported wall shear stress. OpenFOAM wall-stress outputs may be expressed per unit density; check dimensions before converting them.
Plot \(u^+=u_x/u_\tau\) against \(y^+=yu_\tau/\nu\). Compare with Spalding’s relation,
\[
y^+=u^++\frac{1}{E}\left[e^{\kappa u^+}-1-\kappa u^+-\frac{(\kappa u^+)^2}{2}-\frac{(\kappa u^+)^3}{6}\right],
\]
using \(\kappa=0.41\) and \(E=9.8\) as reference values. Generate the comparison curve parametrically in \(u^+\); a nonlinear inverse is not required for plotting. Treat it as an empirical near-wall reference, not an exact solution throughout the channel.
Compare the reference-case estimates of \(u_\tau/\bar{U}\) against the empirical correlation
\[
\frac{\widehat{u_\tau}}{\bar{U}}=0.169\,Re_b^{-0.115}.
\]
Assess its discrepancy over your sampled range. This is a candidate empirical approximation for this exercise, not a universal friction law. If you fit a replacement, use training cases for fitting and validation cases for choosing its form.


Train and compare a transformed model

Use the deployable estimate \(\widehat{u_\tau}\) to form \(\widehat{y^+}=y\widehat{u_\tau}/\nu\) and the target \(\widehat{u^+}=u_x/\widehat{u_\tau}\). Use the same estimate in training and inference. Reserve CFD-derived \(u_\tau\) for diagnostic plots, rather than silently providing unavailable information at prediction time.
Train a scalar mapping \(\log(\widehat{y^+})\mapsto\widehat{u^+}\) using the same case splits. Cell centers have positive wall distance; reject nonpositive inputs before taking a logarithm. Treat the wall value separately using the no-slip condition.
Fit statistical scalers on training data only. Predict using the full chain: compute \(Re_b\) and \(\widehat{u_\tau}\), transform and scale the input, evaluate the model, invert target scaling, and multiply by \(\widehat{u_\tau}\).
Compare against the direct model and baseline in dimensional velocity units on identical held-out profiles. Do not compare raw losses from differently scaled target spaces as if they measured the same error.
Check where profile collapse works and where omitting Reynolds number loses information. Separate errors from the friction-velocity approximation and errors from the learned mapping as far as your diagnostics allow.




Task 11 — Test extrapolation to unseen Reynolds numbers
The interior test profiles in Task 9 measure interpolation. Now examine predictions outside the training interval, using additional CFD reference cases that remain separate from all model-development data.

Record the minimum and maximum training Reynolds numbers. Select at least one Reynolds number outside this interval before inspecting its reference profile. For example, \(\bar{U}=1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) gives \(Re_b=120{,}000\) for the geometry and viscosity in Task 8, above the full sampling range specified there. Optionally add a lower-Reynolds-number case; discuss whether turbulent-flow assumptions still apply as Reynolds number decreases.
Create a fresh copy of the channel case and set its bulk velocity, time step, and end time consistently with Task 8. Preserve a comparable dimensionless duration as a starting point, then check late-time profile changes and extend the run if necessary. Check mesh adequacy, near-wall resolution, solver logs, final time, and the volume-weighted bulk speed. Record both the solver end time and the time of the reference field. A new Reynolds number can require different numerical resolution or run duration.
Freeze the models before evaluation: keep network parameters, architecture, activation, statistical scalers, friction-velocity correlation, and baseline training profiles unchanged. Do not refit normalization or use the new CFD solution to supply friction velocity to the wall-scaled model. If any model-development choices are changed after inspecting these results, classify this case as development data and generate another untouched case for testing.
Predict the new profile with the piecewise linear baseline, direct MLP, and wall-scaled MLP. For the baseline, use the linear extension from the nearest two training profiles. For the MLPs, apply the complete input and output transformations from Tasks 9 and 10 without clipping inputs to the training range.
Plot the dimensional velocity profiles and residuals versus wall distance. Report RMSE and maximum absolute error with the same sample weighting used for the interior tests. Include the achieved bulk speed of each predicted profile and variation across the frozen training seeds.
Compare training, validation, interior-test, and extrapolation errors in one table. Explain why the linear baseline’s zero training error and a low interpolation error do not establish extrapolation capability. Identify where the direct MLP’s inputs and the wall-scaled model’s \(\log(\widehat{y^+})\) leave their respective training ranges. Discuss the near-wall and outer-channel regions separately, including limitations of the friction-velocity correlation and wall scaling.

Treat the result as evidence for the tested flow conditions and distance from the training interval. One successful extrapolation case does not establish reliable predictions at arbitrary Reynolds numbers.
