title: Course overview and motivation
Course overview and motivation
text:
Part 1 — Theory

Task 1 — Decompose an application
Choose two of the following situations. Draw a workflow and explain your design; several reasonable approaches are possible.

Find leaks in a water-distribution network. Pressure and flow-rate sensors record several locations in a pipe network. Water demand changes throughout the day, and some sensors occasionally fail. You have records from normal operation and a few controlled leak tests at known locations. You want to detect a leak and narrow down its location without mistaking ordinary changes in demand for a fault.
Choose a cyclone separator design. A cyclone removes solid particles from a gas stream. Simulations and experiments are available for a limited set of geometries, flow rates, and particle-size distributions. The measurements include pressure loss and the fraction of particles collected. You want to select a geometry that meets a specified collection requirement with low pumping power, while limiting the number of additional simulations or experiments.
Operate ventilation in a changing environment. A room has adjustable supply fans and dampers. Sensors measure temperature and carbon-dioxide concentration at several locations, while occupancy and outdoor conditions vary. You have historical operating records and can test candidate strategies in a room-flow simulation. You want to maintain acceptable air quality and comfort while reducing energy consumption.
Plan a large CFD parameter study. Pilot simulations of flow through a porous structure have produced solver logs, numerical settings, mesh statistics, and a few physical output quantities. Some runs converged quickly, some stalled, and some crashed. You want to identify recurring kinds of simulation behaviour and choose settings and computing resources for the remaining cases. A short run should help you decide whether to continue, change the settings, or stop.

For each chosen situation:

Define the physical question and the desired output.
Identify the available data and any additional data you would need. Distinguish snapshots, derived quantities, and secondary data where relevant.
Divide the problem into subproblems. Decide which require regression, classification, dimensionality reduction, clustering, or reinforcement learning, and justify your choices. You do not need to use every category.
Specify the inputs and outputs of each step. For supervised tasks, distinguish features, feature values, targets, and individual samples. For control, specify the state, action, and reward.
Explain where domain knowledge, analytical models, or classical numerical methods could help. Identify information that must survive any reduction step.
Sketch how the steps connect using the extract–learn–use workflows from Lecture 1.
Propose checks that could reveal failure. Consider data coverage, independent test cases, physical consistency, and the consequences of an incorrect prediction or action.



Task 2 — Challenge your proposed workflow
Exchange one design with a partner. Identify one assumption that could fail, one simpler alternative, and one experiment or numerical check that would distinguish the alternatives. Revise your design and state what remains uncertain.
No reference solution is provided. Your aim is to make a credible case for the workflow, rather than merely name an algorithm. Explain your reasoning and use the learning and verification guidance from Lecture 0.

title: Course overview and motivation
section: Part 2 — Practical lab: setting up your system
text:
Part 2 — Practical lab: setting up your system
The course uses Linux for Python, CFD tools, and containers. Choose native Ubuntu, Windows 11 with WSL 2, or Windows 11 with Ubuntu in VirtualBox, then follow the common Ubuntu steps. VirtualBox is an alternative if you have trouble with WSL. The commands below assume an x86-64/AMD64 computer; the legacy course container images and PyTorch wheels may require a different setup on ARM-based devices.
Use Python 3.10 or newer, with Python 3.12 recommended for this course. Ubuntu 26.04 LTS provides Python 3.14 as its default, so Step 4 installs a separate Python 3.12 environment. Python 3.12 is the tested course baseline; Ubuntu’s system Python remains unchanged. A CPU-only installation is sufficient to start; a GPU is not required. Keep space for the Linux distribution, Python packages, container images, and later datasets. The old estimate of 8 GB for the tools alone is not a reliable allowance for the full course.

Step 1 — Get access to Ubuntu

Windows 11: install WSL 2
Install Windows updates, then open PowerShell as administrator:
wsl --list --online
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-26.04
Restart if requested, open Ubuntu, and create your Linux username and password. Check from PowerShell:
wsl --update
wsl --list --verbose
Ubuntu should show VERSION 2. To convert an existing version-1 installation, use its exact distribution name:
wsl --set-version Ubuntu-26.04 2
These commands follow Microsoft’s WSL installation guide. From this point onward, run Linux commands in the Ubuntu terminal, not PowerShell.


Windows 11: install Ubuntu in VirtualBox
In this route, Windows is the host and Ubuntu is the guest. Run the course’s terminal commands, Python environment, editor, and CFD simulations inside Ubuntu. You can use Windows ParaView to inspect completed results copied into a shared folder.

Download the current stable Windows installer from the official VirtualBox download page, run it, and restart Windows if requested. The base package is sufficient for this workflow.
Download the Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS Desktop AMD64 ISO from Ubuntu. This is the installer used in the course’s VM test.
Open VirtualBox and create a new VM named ML-CFD-Ubuntu. Select the Ubuntu ISO and Linux / Ubuntu (64-bit). Choose manual installation (skip unattended installation) so that you create your own Ubuntu account and install Guest Additions using Ubuntu packages below.
Allocate 4 CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, and an 80 GB dynamically allocated virtual disk. A Windows computer with at least 16 GB RAM is a practical starting point; leave enough memory and CPU capacity for Windows. The disk grows as files are added, up to its configured limit. Allow additional space for the installer and later datasets.
Keep the network adapter on NAT for internet access. Use VMSVGA graphics with 128 MB video memory; 3D acceleration and nested virtualization are not required for the tested setup.
Start the VM and install Ubuntu. Choose your language, keyboard, time zone, username, and password. The installer’s disk selection refers to the VM’s virtual disk. Restart into the installed Ubuntu system and remove the installer ISO from the virtual optical drive if requested.

Inside the installed Ubuntu desktop, open a terminal and install Ubuntu’s packaged Guest Additions:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install virtualbox-guest-utils virtualbox-guest-x11
sudo usermod -aG vboxsf "$USER"
sudo reboot
Use this package route for the course VM. In the local test, the Guest Additions ISO bundled with VirtualBox 7.2.6 failed to build a module against Ubuntu’s updated kernel; the Ubuntu packages worked after reboot. If you already installed Guest Additions from an ISO, ask the teaching team before replacing that installation.
Create a shared folder:

On Windows, create a folder such as C:\Users\YOUR_NAME\ML-CFD-share, replacing YOUR_NAME with your Windows username.
Shut down Ubuntu. In VirtualBox, open the VM’s Settings → Shared Folders and add that Windows folder. Set the Folder Name to ML-CFD-share, enable Auto-mount, leave Read-only unchecked, and save it as a permanent machine folder.
Start Ubuntu again. The folder should be available at /media/sf_ML-CFD-share.
In Ubuntu, verify that you can write a file:
printf 'Written inside Ubuntu\n' > /media/sf_ML-CFD-share/guest-check.txt
Open guest-check.txt from the Windows folder. Create another text file there using Windows, then open it from /media/sf_ML-CFD-share in Ubuntu. Repeat the check after a reboot.

Keep the course checkout, Python environments, SIF images, and running simulation cases in Ubuntu’s home directory. Use the shared folder to exchange scripts, plots, and completed results. See VirtualBox’s shared-folder documentation.
Continue with Step 2 in the Ubuntu guest terminal. All later Ubuntu commands apply inside this VM. If VirtualBox reports unavailable hardware virtualization, check the manufacturer’s firmware instructions. VirtualBox can coexist with Windows Hyper-V, but performance can vary; use Oracle’s troubleshooting guide to diagnose the reported issue.


Native Linux
If you already use Ubuntu 26.04, continue below. Otherwise, follow the Ubuntu installation guide. Installing a second operating system involves disk partitioning; WSL 2 and VirtualBox avoid that step on Windows 11.



Step 2 — Install basic tools, including the compiler
In Ubuntu:
sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
sudo apt install git build-essential python3 python3-venv python3-pip python3-dev software-properties-common cmake wget unzip openmpi-bin
A minimal WSL installation may lack a compiler. Install build-essential; you do not need to compile GCC yourself. It supplies GCC, G++, Make, and supporting development packages. Check:
gcc --version
g++ --version
make --version
python3 --version
command -v mpirun
The system Python should report 3.14 on Ubuntu 26.04. The course environment created below uses Python 3.12 instead. See Ubuntu’s build-essential package.
openmpi-bin supplies the Linux MPI launcher used by the course’s parallel CFD scripts. Install it in Ubuntu even when OpenFOAM runs in Apptainer: RunFunctions launches mpirun outside the container. The Ubuntu 26.04 launcher and the course container passed a two-process test together.


Step 3 — Clone the course into the Linux home directory
mkdir -p ~/Development
cd ~/Development
git clone https://github.com/AndreWeiner/ml-cfd-lecture.git
cd ml-cfd-lecture
mkdir -p exercises
If you already have a checkout, use it rather than cloning again. Keep your own work in exercises/, which is ignored by Git. Run git pull from the repository root to receive updates; inspect your local changes before resolving any conflicts.
With WSL, keep the checkout under ~/Development, rather than /mnt/c/..., for Linux filesystem performance and permissions. Open the current folder in Windows Explorer with explorer.exe .. See Microsoft’s filesystem guidance.
With VirtualBox, use the same ~/Development location inside Ubuntu, rather than /media/sf_ML-CFD-share. Edit and run your work inside the VM; copy completed results to the shared folder for Windows access.


Step 4 — Create the Python environment
From the repository root, install uv in a small tools environment and use it to download Python 3.12 and create the course environment:
python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/course-tools
~/.venvs/course-tools/bin/python -m pip install --upgrade uv
~/.venvs/course-tools/bin/uv venv --python 3.12 --seed ml-cfd
source ml-cfd/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install torch==2.14.1 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pip check
uv downloads a managed Python interpreter when the requested version is missing. See its Python installation guide. No Python compilation or replacement of Ubuntu’s system Python is required. After activation, check python --version; it should report 3.12.
The CPU installation follows PyTorch’s version-specific instructions. We retain PyTorch 2.14.1 because the course’s OpenFOAM container and manual setup use LibTorch 2.14.1. Do not independently upgrade one side of that pairing. Most other packages remain unpinned, so successful dependency resolution and the checks below are important. The course uses torch.export for model export. Older exercises may still contain TorchScript calls until they are revised. Later examples will need their own compatibility checks.
Install the latest available FlowTorch release from PyPI. The distribution is named flowtorch-fluid, while Python imports remain flowtorch. The latest published release checked for this revision is 1.9.0; install the all extra to include the data loaders, reduced-order modelling, and pressure-sensitive-paint dependencies:
python -m pip install --upgrade "flowtorch-fluid[all]"
See FlowTorch’s package instructions. The removed aweiner Git branch is no longer used. Newer releases may change behavior, so record the installed version and check each later application with its required data.
In each new terminal, reactivate the environment:
cd ~/Development/ml-cfd-lecture
source ml-cfd/bin/activate
Use python -m pip inside this environment; do not install course Python packages with sudo pip. Leave the environment with deactivate.


Step 5 — Verify Python and run a small script
Save the following as exercises/setup_check.py:
import sys
import warnings
from importlib.metadata import version
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas
import sklearn
import torch
# Some dependencies currently import legacy TorchScript code internally.
# Hide only its known deprecation warning; this check uses torch.export.
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.filterwarnings(
        "ignore", message=r"`torch\.jit\.script` is deprecated\..*",
        category=FutureWarning, module=r"torch\.jit\._script",
    )
    import botorch
    import gpytorch
    import flowtorch
    from flowtorch import DATASETS
    from flowtorch.data import FOAMDataloader, mask_box

print("Python:", sys.version.split()[0])
print("Interpreter:", sys.executable)
print("PyTorch:", torch.__version__)
print("FlowTorch:", version("flowtorch-fluid"))
assert torch.__version__.split("+")[0] == "2.14.1"
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
assert torch.isclose(x.mean(), torch.tensor(2.0))

class ExampleModel(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        return x.square() + 1.0

model = ExampleModel().eval()
exported = torch.export.export(model, (x,))
torch.testing.assert_close(exported.module()(x), torch.tensor([2.0, 5.0, 10.0]))
export_path = Path(__file__).with_name("setup-check.pt2")
torch.export.save(exported, export_path)
loaded = torch.export.load(export_path)
test_input = torch.tensor([0.0, -2.0, 4.0])
torch.testing.assert_close(loaded.module()(test_input), torch.tensor([1.0, 5.0, 17.0]))
print("PyTorch export, save/load, and inference passed:", export_path)

t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, np.sin(t))
ax.set(xlabel="t", ylabel="sin(t)")
path = Path(__file__).with_name("setup-check.png")
fig.savefig(path)
plt.close(fig)
print("Saved:", path)
print("Core package imports, PyTorch export, and basic calculations passed.")
Run it from the repository root:
python exercises/setup_check.py
Inspect the saved sine curve. The script also exports a small model, saves it as setup-check.pt2, reloads it, and checks its predictions against known values. Some third-party dependencies still import legacy TorchScript code internally, so the script suppresses only that specific warning during those imports. These checks confirm imports, model export, and basic execution, not the correctness of every later course example. FlowTorch’s example datasets are separate from the Python package; later chapters explain which data are needed.
The course sources are Python scripts with # %% cells. You can run your own scripts from the terminal or use an editor that supports individual cells. JupyterLab is optional:
cd exercises
jupyter lab --no-browser
Open the printed localhost URL, including its token, in your Windows browser for WSL, or your Ubuntu browser for native Linux and VirtualBox. In VirtualBox, localhost refers to the Ubuntu guest, so use the browser inside the VM. Keep the server terminal open; stop it with Ctrl+C. The browser token is private. You do not need JupyterLab to run ordinary Python scripts.


Step 6 — Install the latest stable ParaView
Use the latest stable binary from the official ParaView download page, rather than Ubuntu’s potentially older apt package. The latest stable release checked on 12 October 2026 is 6.2.0; avoid nightly builds and release candidates for the course.
On Windows 11, install the Windows AMD64 package. With WSL, open case files through the WSL filesystem in Explorer. With VirtualBox, copy the complete case directory from Ubuntu into /media/sf_ML-CFD-share, then open its .foam file from the corresponding Windows folder. A .foam file is only a marker; keep constant, system, and the saved time directories beside it. Reconstruct parallel results before copying, as shown after the container installation below. This keeps visualization on Windows while CFD runs in Ubuntu.
You can also run ParaView inside native Ubuntu or the VirtualBox guest. Download the Linux x86-64 archive and install the GUI libraries that were missing on a fresh Ubuntu desktop. For the verified 6.2.0 archive, installation and launch are:
sudo apt install libxkbcommon-x11-0 libxcb-cursor0 libxcb-icccm4 libxcb-image0 libxcb-keysyms1 libxcb-render-util0 libxcb-xkb1
mkdir -p ~/Applications
tar -xzf ~/Downloads/ParaView-6.2.0-MPI-Linux-Python3.12-x86_64.tar.gz -C ~/Applications
~/Applications/ParaView-6.2.0-MPI-Linux-Python3.12-x86_64/bin/pvpython --version
QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb ~/Applications/ParaView-6.2.0-MPI-Linux-Python3.12-x86_64/bin/paraview
Run the GUI command from a terminal in the Ubuntu desktop. QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb selects the X11 backend included in this binary, also when Ubuntu uses a Wayland desktop. The library packages above are needed only for Linux ParaView, not Windows ParaView.
If the download page offers a newer stable release, use its corresponding archive and directory names. ParaView includes its own Python runtime; do not add its Python packages to the course environment’s PYTHONPATH.
Linux GUI applications can also run through WSLg on supported Windows 11 installations. See Microsoft’s WSL GUI guidance.


Step 7 — Install Apptainer
In Ubuntu, install Apptainer from its official PPA:
sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:apptainer/ppa
sudo apt update
sudo apt install apptainer
apptainer --version
apptainer exec docker://alpine cat /etc/alpine-release
This uses prebuilt packages and avoids compiling Go or Apptainer. The final command should print the container’s Alpine release. The Apptainer installation guide documents this installation route and WSL 2 support.
In VirtualBox, Apptainer runs inside Ubuntu and uses the guest’s Linux kernel. Store SIF images on Ubuntu’s disk and run them as your ordinary Ubuntu user. No additional VM or nested hardware virtualization is required. The tested PPA installation ran containers with Ubuntu’s default user-namespace restrictions; no system-wide security-setting changes were needed.


Step 8 — Set up OpenFOAM and LibTorch
Choose Route A (container) or Route B (manual installation) for OpenFOAM/LibTorch. Both use OpenFOAM.com v2606 and CPU LibTorch 2.14.1. Do not mix the OpenFOAM.com and OpenFOAM Foundation distributions when following these commands.

Route A — Pull the course Apptainer container
The container uses Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS as its base, with OpenFOAM.com v2606 and CPU LibTorch 2.14.1. It runs in Ubuntu on native Linux, WSL 2, or VirtualBox. Download the tested image from GitHub Container Registry into the course repository root, then run the acceptance checks:
cd ~/Development/ml-cfd-lecture
apptainer pull of2606-py2.14.1-cpu.sif \
  oras://ghcr.io/andreweiner/of-pytorch:of2606-libtorch2.14.1-ubuntu26.04-cpu
apptainer run of2606-py2.14.1-cpu.sif simpleFoam -help
apptainer run of2606-py2.14.1-cpu.sif /opt/of-pytorch-tests/run-tests.sh
source setup-env
Use oras:// for this registry artifact; it is an Apptainer SIF image. The runscript activates OpenFOAM automatically. You do not need to build the container yourself. source setup-env selects this image and OpenFOAM version for the course scripts; run it again from the repository root in each new terminal used for CFD exercises.
Later: copy parallel CFD results to Windows ParaView. After completing a cylinder simulation in the CFD exercise, reconstruct its time directories inside Ubuntu, then copy the case into the VirtualBox shared folder:
cd ~/Development/ml-cfd-lecture
source setup-env
cd exercises/cylinder2D
apptainer exec "$ML_CFD_IMAGE" bash -c 'source /usr/lib/openfoam/openfoam2606/etc/bashrc && reconstructPar'
cp -r "$PWD" /media/sf_ML-CFD-share/
Open cylinder2D/post.foam from the Windows shared folder in ParaView, choose Reconstructed Case, and click Apply. Adjust the directory name if you used another case. For a later transfer, choose a fresh destination or replace the previous copy deliberately so that obsolete time directories are not mixed with new results.
If you prefer to build it locally, the definition and compilation examples are included in containers/of_pytorch/. From the course repository root:
cd containers/of_pytorch
apptainer build --fakeroot of2606-py2.14.1-cpu.sif Singularity.def
cd ../..
cp containers/of_pytorch/of2606-py2.14.1-cpu.sif .
The build compiles and runs the C++ examples. If fakeroot is unavailable on your computer, use sudo apptainer build instead.
The container contains LibTorch, the C++ frontend; your Python virtual environment remains in Ubuntu outside the container. For an interactive container shell, activate OpenFOAM explicitly:
apptainer shell of2606-py2.14.1-cpu.sif
source /usr/lib/openfoam/openfoam2606/etc/bashrc


Route B — Install OpenFOAM and LibTorch manually
Run these commands in Ubuntu, including Ubuntu inside WSL 2. Download and inspect the official repository setup script before running it:
wget -O /tmp/add-openfoam-repo.sh https://dl.openfoam.com/add-debian-repo.sh
less /tmp/add-openfoam-repo.sh
sudo bash /tmp/add-openfoam-repo.sh
sudo apt update
sudo apt install openfoam2606-dev
source /usr/lib/openfoam/openfoam2606/etc/bashrc
simpleFoam -help
wmake -help
This installs precompiled OpenFOAM packages and their development files; it does not compile OpenFOAM from source. See the OpenFOAM.com release and installation links.
Install the CPU LibTorch archive into your home directory:
mkdir -p ~/Applications
cd ~/Applications
wget -O libtorch-2.14.1-cpu.zip 'https://download.pytorch.org/libtorch/cpu/libtorch-shared-with-deps-2.14.1%2Bcpu.zip'
echo '0f02329a5266153cffa9dc12926ff2221fa626207b894d40bd61905cc2079821  libtorch-2.14.1-cpu.zip' | sha256sum -c -
mkdir -p libtorch-2.14.1
unzip libtorch-2.14.1-cpu.zip -d libtorch-2.14.1
export TORCH_LIBRARIES="$HOME/Applications/libtorch-2.14.1/libtorch"
cat "$TORCH_LIBRARIES/build-version"
The checksum records the official archive used for this revision. Avoid unpacking over an existing installation. See PyTorch’s LibTorch installation guide.
For each terminal used to compile OpenFOAM/LibTorch code, source OpenFOAM’s etc/bashrc and set TORCH_LIBRARIES as above. LibTorch 2.14.1 requires C++20. The examples select it per application without modifying OpenFOAM’s global compiler rules. Include LibTorch headers before OpenFOAM headers to avoid the TypeName macro clash.
Verify the combined toolchain from the course root:
cd ~/Development/ml-cfd-lecture
source /usr/lib/openfoam/openfoam2606/etc/bashrc
export TORCH_LIBRARIES="$HOME/Applications/libtorch-2.14.1/libtorch"
bash containers/of_pytorch/test/run-tests.sh
This compiles and runs both the wmake tensor example and the CMake neural-network example. The checks include an analytical derivative comparison, tensor serialization, and output shape and finite-value checks.


Basilisk for later exercises
The existing Basilisk exercise still uses its separate container:
apptainer pull basilisk.sif docker://andreweiner/basilisk:20-11-19
apptainer exec basilisk.sif sh -c 'command -v qcc; gcc --version'
The first CFD exercise will compile and run the provided Basilisk solver. Listing the compiler does not yet validate that simulation. Record download or execution failures and contact the teaching team rather than substituting an arbitrary image.



Step 9 — Optional editor setup
With WSL, install Visual Studio Code on Windows, add the WSL extension, and open the course from an Ubuntu terminal with code .. Install the Python extension in the WSL environment and select ml-cfd/bin/python as the interpreter. On native Ubuntu or inside the VirtualBox guest, install the Linux edition of VS Code using its Ubuntu instructions, open ~/Development/ml-cfd-lecture, and select that same course interpreter. See VS Code’s WSL guide.


Step 10 — Optional: OpenCode with ScaDS.AI models (TUD:AI)
This step is optional. You can complete the practical lab without a coding agent.
Before using a coding agent, read Topic 0 — How to learn with generative AI for guidance on using AI tools while developing your own understanding and checking their output.

Install OpenCode Desktop

Windows 11: On the official OpenCode download page, select OpenCode Desktop → Windows (x64). Run the downloaded installer and start OpenCode from the Start menu.
Ubuntu Linux: On the same page, download the Linux (.deb) package. Open a terminal in the download folder and install that file with sudo apt install ./NAME.deb, replacing NAME.deb with its actual filename. Start OpenCode from the applications menu.

With VirtualBox, use the Linux installation inside Ubuntu, even though the laptop runs Windows. Open the repository in Ubuntu’s home directory so that the agent can use the Linux course environment.
Open your ml-cfd-lecture repository folder as the project in OpenCode. Keep your own exercise scripts and generated results in exercises.


Create a TU Dresden API key

Open the TUD:AI LLM service in the TU Dresden Self-Service Portal.
Sign in with your TU Dresden account and select Manage API access (German: API-Zugang verwalten).
Follow the portal’s prompts to create a key and accept the service’s usage terms.
Keep the key private. Enter it only in the agent’s provider connection; do not put it in exercise scripts, shared screenshots, or a Git repository.

The public service description currently lists employees as the eligible group, while the TUD:AI documentation describes access for TU Dresden affiliates more broadly. If API access is unavailable for your student account, ask the lecturer or tutor about course access and continue without the optional agent. See the TUD:AI documentation for service details.


Connect OpenCode to ScaDS.AI models
Create opencode.json in the repository root. This local configuration is excluded from Git tracking. It sets GLM 5.3 Flash as the default and includes GLM 5.3 and Qwen3.8 27B as alternatives for course work.
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "model": "scads/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash",
  "provider": {
    "scads": {
      "name": "TUD:AI",
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://llm.scads.ai/v1"
      },
      "models": {
        "zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash": {
          "name": "GLM 5.3 Flash",
          "limit": {
            "context": 1048576,
            "output": 32768
          }
        },
        "zai-org/GLM-5.3": {
          "name": "GLM 5.3",
          "limit": {
            "context": 524288,
            "output": 32768
          }
        },
        "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B": {
          "name": "Qwen3.8 27B",
          "limit": {
            "context": 262144,
            "output": 32768
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
Models can change or become unavailable. Check the TUD:AI model availability page to see which models are currently available, and update the model identifiers in this configuration if necessary. The default model uses the format provider/model-id.
Restart the project after saving the configuration. Open the provider connection dialog (/connect in the command interface), choose TUD:AI (provider ID scads), and enter your portal key. If you need to add it as a custom provider, use the same provider ID, scads. Use the model picker (/models in the command interface) to switch between the configured models.
The configuration contains no API key. Requests use the TUD:AI endpoint. See the OpenCode custom-provider guide for further configuration details.
On Windows, course Python commands must run inside Ubuntu in WSL or VirtualBox. Check the command and interpreter path before allowing the agent to run it.
For a first check, ask the agent to explain exercises/setup_check.py. Tell it to use the Python interpreter inside ml-cfd when running course code. Read its suggestions and verify the result yourself.



Troubleshooting Windows 11 and Ubuntu







Symptom
What to check




WSL installation remains at 0%.
Try wsl --install --web-download -d Ubuntu-26.04 in administrator PowerShell.


Ubuntu reports version 1.
Convert the exact distribution name using wsl --set-version NAME 2.


A required virtualization feature is missing, for example error 0x80370102 or 0x80370114.
Check that Virtual Machine Platform is enabled, hardware virtualization is enabled in the firmware, and Windows has restarted. Follow the manufacturer’s firmware instructions.


Error 0x8007019e reports that WSL is not enabled.
Enable the Windows Subsystem for Linux component in Windows features and restart.


A kernel update is requested.
Run wsl --update, then wsl --shutdown, and reopen Ubuntu. The manual kernel MSI belongs to the older installation route.


gcc, g++, or make is missing.
Install build-essential inside Ubuntu; a Windows compiler does not supply Linux build tools.


Parallel CFD logs report mpirun: command not found.
Install openmpi-bin inside Ubuntu, then retry in a fresh copy of the case. Existing log files can cause the course scripts to skip a previous failed step.


The VirtualBox shared folder is missing or access is denied.
Check the permanent folder name ML-CFD-share, Auto-mount, Ubuntu’s virtualbox-guest-utils package, and membership of vboxsf using id. Reboot after adding group membership.


ParaView on Ubuntu reports that the Qt xcb plugin cannot load.
Install the GUI libraries listed in Step 6 and launch from the Ubuntu desktop using QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb.


Apptainer cannot download an image and reports HTTP 500.
Preserve the error and retry once; a registry error can be temporary. Check the exact image URI and contact the teaching team if it persists.


venv creation fails or pip reports an externally managed environment.
Install python3-venv for the tools environment, then create ml-cfd with ~/.venvs/course-tools/bin/uv venv --python 3.12 --seed ml-cfd as in Step 4 and activate it.


Python cannot import a course package.
Check which python, reactivate ml-cfd, and run python -m pip check. Preserve any dependency-conflict messages.


Linux file operations are slow or permissions behave unexpectedly.
Move the checkout and simulation cases into the Linux home directory.


Jupyter does not open a browser automatically.
Use jupyter lab --no-browser and open its printed localhost URL manually. With VirtualBox, open it in Ubuntu’s browser.



For WSL errors, use Microsoft’s troubleshooting guide. Diagnose the reported problem rather than disabling Windows security features or reinstalling the distribution.


Validation of the VirtualBox route
On 14 October 2026, a fresh Ubuntu 26.04.1 Desktop guest was tested on a Linux host with VirtualBox 7.2.6, using 4 cores and 8 GB RAM. The Python 3.12 environment, CPU PyTorch 2.14.1, FlowTorch 1.9.0, Apptainer 1.5.4, container C++ checks, and JupyterLab startup passed. With openmpi-bin installed, the cylinder workflow passed a short two-process run, mesh checking, and reconstruction. Shared-folder access worked in both directions after reboot; host ParaView 6.2 read and rendered the copied case. The guest ParaView GUI started after installing the listed libraries.
This validates the Ubuntu guest workflow. Installation on a physical Windows host, Windows ParaView, optional editors/agents, and the full-duration CFD benchmark were not tested. The short simulation checks tool execution and readable output; later exercises still require their own numerical checks.


Completion record
Record your operating system, WSL or VirtualBox version if applicable, Ubuntu version, Python and PyTorch versions, compiler version, Apptainer version, and the outcome of each check. For VirtualBox, also record the assigned CPU cores/RAM and the shared-folder check after reboot. Include the plot and any unresolved errors. Be prepared to explain which tools run on Windows, which run in Ubuntu, and which run inside a container.

text:
Keep understanding alongside output
AI can explain unfamiliar ideas, give feedback, generate practice questions, and help you explore code. A completed task is only one measure of success. Ask yourself: What can I now explain or do that I could not do before?
Some struggle is essential for learning. Recalling ideas, trying an approach, making mistakes, and diagnosing them require effort that no AI can do for you. You do not need to remain stuck indefinitely: use AI to help you take the next step, then do that step yourself.
Watching someone else—or an AI—solve a problem is not the same as solving it yourself. An explanation can seem clear while you are following it. You discover which parts you have understood and where gaps remain only when you apply the concept independently. Practise this throughout the course; by the exam, you need to be able to reason and solve problems yourself.
Learning takes time, repeated recall, and regular practice. Working through a problem once—even with real effort—is not enough. Return to the topic on different days, try to recall the reasoning without looking at a solution, and apply it to new problems. You may get stuck or make mistakes again; identify what went wrong, then try again. Continue practising until you can explain the concept and use it with increasing ease. Consider your understanding satisfactory only when you can return to a problem after some time and still recall and apply the reasoning with ease and without assistance. Solving it immediately after seeing an explanation is not enough. Make this a regular habit throughout the course rather than leaving it until just before the exam.
Understanding the subject also helps you use AI effectively. You need enough knowledge to ask useful questions, judge whether an answer makes sense, recognise mistakes, and guide the tool when it goes wrong. Without that understanding, you can accept plausible but incorrect results or become stuck because you cannot tell why the output is unsatisfactory. Developing your own expertise therefore remains essential when working with AI.

text:
A practical learning cycle
Attempt → ask → examine → practise independently → revisit.

Choose a learning goal. Identify the skill you are practising. If you are learning a discretization, develop its core yourself. If you already understand a routine task, delegating it can leave more time for the harder parts.
Make an attempt. Write down your approach, prediction, or first few steps before asking for help.
Ask for targeted assistance. Request one hint, a simpler example, or feedback on your reasoning. Work through the response and challenge anything unclear.
Check the result. Design checks that could reveal mistakes, including mistakes in AI output.
Close the tool. Explain the idea, solve a related problem, or recreate a small implementation without assistance. Return to it later to check what you remember.

Use chat tools as interactive tutors
Give the tool your reasoning and ask it to help you improve it. For example:

Give me one hint, then wait for my attempt.


Here is my reasoning. Identify the first mistake without completing the solution.


Quiz me one question at a time about boundary conditions, and ask me to justify my answer.


I have expanded this vector equation into Cartesian components. Ask me questions that help me find errors rather than rewriting it for me.

Explain the answer in your own words afterwards. Recognising a convincing explanation is easier than producing one yourself.
If the exercises provided in the course are not sufficient for your practice, use AI to generate additional exercises on the same topic. Ask for variations and gradually increasing difficulty, and attempt them before requesting hints or feedback. Check that the generated tasks are clear and consistent with the course assumptions; AI-generated exercises can contain mistakes too.

Generate three additional exercises on this topic, starting at the level of the course exercises and increasing the difficulty. Give me only the questions first, without solutions, and wait for my attempt.

Use coding agents in understandable steps
Describe the intended behaviour and sketch your approach before requesting changes. Ask for a plan, keep changes small, review them, and predict what the code will do before running it. Practise writing and debugging the parts central to your learning goal yourself.
For example:

Help me diagnose this failure. Ask for my hypothesis first, suggest a diagnostic check, and wait before editing.


I want to implement a finite-difference approximation myself. Review my indexing and boundary treatment, but do not replace the implementation.

An agent can help with routine setup or plotting once you understand the task. You should still be able to explain the code, its assumptions, and its limitations. A successful run alone does not establish that it solves the intended problem.

section: Build your own evidence of correctness
text:
Build your own evidence of correctness
No reference solutions will be provided in this course. Developing and defending a verification strategy is part of the course. You are responsible for checking your work, including anything produced by AI.
Use several checks that can reveal different kinds of mistakes:







Check
Example in fluid mechanics or scientific computing




Predict before running
Sketch the expected profile and estimate its magnitude or sign.


Construct simple cases
Work out a small mesh by hand, or test a case with a simple analytical solution.


Check limits and consistency
Check units, signs, boundary conditions, symmetry, conservation, and limiting parameter values.


Examine refinement
Compare several mesh spacings and examine whether the result approaches a stable limit. However, note that a stable limit alone does not guarantee the correct model or solution.


Compare independent approaches
Compare a derivation, a simpler model, or a separate implementation that does not merely copy the same logic.


Try to break the solution
Search for inputs or counterexamples that expose incorrect assumptions or indexing.



AI can suggest checks, but you must explain why they are meaningful and examine the results yourself. Asking the same tool whether its answer is correct provides little independent evidence.
In this course, we will also work on defining skills for AI agents: reusable instructions and procedures that help agents carry out some of these checks systematically. You must still develop and choose meaningful checks yourself, drawing on your understanding of the problem and the experience you gain through practice. A skill can help implement a verification strategy, but deciding what needs to be checked and interpreting the evidence remain your responsibility.
Report what you checked, what the evidence supports, and what remains uncertain. Passing checks increases confidence; it does not guarantee correctness.

title: Course overview and motivation
Course overview and motivation
section: Why do machine learning and fluid mechanics complement each other?
text:
Why do machine learning and fluid mechanics complement each other?
Fluid mechanics provides data and questions about fluid motion. Machine learning provides methods for learning from those data. The two fields meet both when we analyze a flow and when we build a model of it.







Fluid mechanics
Machine learning




Experiments and simulations produce complex data. They generate large volumes of data, often with high spatial and temporal resolution. Three-dimensional, time-dependent flow fields are particularly difficult to analyze and turn into physical understanding.
Machine learning finds patterns in complex data. It is the science of making computers learn from data rather than explicitly programming every rule. Its methods can identify relationships and structure in high-dimensional datasets.


Fluid mechanics requires data for models. Parameters in material models are fitted to reference data. Turbulence models in CFD require calibration against high-fidelity experiments or simulations.
Machine learning creates useful representations of data. Learned models can represent relationships between quantities, estimate model parameters, and make predictions for inputs for which measurements or simulations are unavailable.




How large can flow datasets become?
The following examples from direct numerical simulations of turbulent flow give an idea of the storage required for a single flow snapshot. A time-resolved dataset contains many such snapshots.



Year
Source
Approximate snapshot size




1987
J. Kim, P. Moin, R. D. Moser
~30 MB


1999
R. D. Moser, J. Kim, N. N. Mansour
~290 MB


2015
M. Lee, R. D. Moser
~900 GB


2025
P. K. Yeung et al.
~500 TB



The first three illustrative estimates come from turbulent channel-flow simulations; the fourth comes from a simulation of isotropic turbulence. Storage depends on the spatial resolution, the number of stored fields, numerical precision, and file format; the values are not the sizes of the complete datasets.


What makes a pattern useful?
A pattern may be a relationship between variables, a recurring spatial structure, or a compact representation of many measurements. Finding a pattern does not automatically provide physical understanding: we still need to ask what it represents and whether it helps answer our question.
Some algorithms learn representations that predict efficiently and accurately but are difficult for humans to interpret. Others seek patterns that are easier to understand, such as a few dominant flow structures or a simple relationship between physical quantities. Which approach is preferable depends on the task: predicting a force and explaining a flow mechanism can place different demands on a model.


From complex flow fields to physical understanding
Direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves the spatial and temporal scales of turbulent motion and can provide detailed reference data for models that represent unresolved turbulence. Large-eddy simulations and Reynolds-averaged simulations also produce flow fields that require systematic analysis. Visual inspection alone rarely reveals all the useful relationships in a large, time-dependent dataset.
A useful representation can be much simpler than the flow itself. For example, the mean streamwise velocity in a turbulent wall-bounded flow follows an approximately logarithmic profile within the logarithmic region, despite the complexity of the instantaneous motion. This illustrates the kind of compact physical relationship we seek; it is not itself a result of machine learning.
Such understanding can guide engineering decisions. A model of shock-induced buffet on an airfoil may help identify ways to reduce unsteady loads. In other applications, understanding a flow mechanism may help enhance a desired effect, such as heat transfer through buoyancy-driven convection. Machine learning can help extract candidate structures or relationships, whose physical meaning must then be examined.


From reference data to fluid-mechanical models
Fluid-mechanical models need information from observations. Even a simulation of a Newtonian fluid requires material properties such as viscosity. Additional physical and turbulence models introduce closure relations and parameters that must be calibrated and validated against suitable reference data.
Initial and boundary conditions also matter. Experimental measurements or high-fidelity simulations can help describe realistic inflow conditions, for example. These data may be noisy, incomplete, or too large to use directly during a simulation. Machine learning can provide compact representations that are easier to evaluate and incorporate into a model. The representation must retain the information relevant to the application, and its effect on the simulation must be checked.


What data are relevant in fluid mechanics?
We have used the term data without specifying what it includes. Common datasets in fluid mechanics fall into three broad groups.

Snapshots of the flow state
A snapshot records the flow state at a particular time instance. In a numerical simulation, it is the discrete solution at that time; an experiment may provide measurements of part of the state. Typical quantities include velocity, pressure, temperature, and other fields relevant to the problem. Collecting snapshots at different times gives a time-resolved dataset.
Snapshots may cover the entire volume or only a subvolume. We may also record or analyze values on boundaries or on slices through the domain. A dataset can therefore contain a complete flow state or only selected quantities and locations.


Derived quantities
We can compute additional quantities from instantaneous flow fields:

Averages, such as time-averaged velocity fields or spatially averaged temperatures.
Integral quantities, such as forces and force coefficients obtained by integrating surface stresses.
Differences between locations or regions, such as pressure losses or temperature differences between inlet and outlet.
Derivatives and quantities based on them, such as vorticity, the curl of the velocity vector: \(\boldsymbol{\omega}=\nabla\times\mathbf{u}\).

These quantities often emphasize information relevant to a particular question. For example, analyzing or visualizing vorticity can help identify rotational structures in a flow, while force coefficients summarize the loading on a body.


Secondary data: how a simulation behaves
Data about the numerical process can be useful too. Examples include log-file messages, residuals of linear solvers and pressure–velocity coupling iterations, numerical settings, iteration counts, and execution times.
Such data help investigate why a simulation converges or fails, why one setup runs faster than another, or why a calculation crashes. Comparing them across runs can reveal relationships between settings, computational cost, and robustness. Solver residuals describe numerical convergence; they do not by themselves establish the physical accuracy of the flow solution.



What is required to combine machine learning and fluid mechanics?
Combining the two fields requires knowledge from three disciplines. Their overlap lets us formulate meaningful questions, choose suitable learning methods, and work efficiently with flow data.
 
The overlaps are conceptual; the circle sizes do not represent quantitative shares.
The table gives only a few representative examples relevant to this course; it could be extended considerably.







Discipline
Examples and their role




Domain knowledge
Domain knowledge includes fundamental fluid-mechanical relationships, numerical techniques, and measurement techniques. It is essential for interpreting data from simulations and experiments, recognizing their limitations, and using them meaningfully in machine learning.


Mathematics
Linear algebra provides tools for modal analysis (finding understandable patterns). Probability theory provides a foundation for deriving probabilistic models. Optimization allows us to fit models and solve design or control problems.


Computer science
Computer science provides efficient algorithms, high-performance and parallel computing methods, data structures, and data-processing techniques. These tools allow us to handle the large datasets illustrated above within the available memory, storage, and computing resources.



Data handling should be planned early, ideally before a simulation begins. Decide which quantities and locations to record, how frequently to store them, and which processing can be performed while the simulation runs. These choices affect both the cost of handling the data and the questions we can answer afterwards.

title: Course overview and motivation
section: Types of problems that ML solves
text:
Types of problems that ML solves
Solving problems in fluid mechanics involves physical, mathematical, and numerical modeling. Machine learning can address particular subproblems when suitable data are available or can be generated. The following categories provide a useful starting point for identifying the learning tasks within an application.

Supervised learning
In supervised learning, we learn a mapping from inputs to outputs using examples for which both are known. The input variables are called features, and the output variable we want to predict is called the target. Each sample, or training example, contains feature values and a corresponding target value, often called a label. The term label is especially common in classification; in regression, we usually refer to a target value. Two common supervised-learning tasks are regression and classification.

Regression
Regression predicts a continuous quantity from one or more features. For example, we may predict the force on a bluff body based on the Reynolds number. In the sketch below, we represent the drag force through its dimensionless drag coefficient. The Reynolds number is the feature and the drag coefficient is the target. A training example might pair a feature value of \(\mathrm{Re}=500\) with a target value of \(c_D=1.2\).
The sketch below shows observations and a regression model that represents their relationship. Once fitted, the model can predict a drag coefficient at Reynolds numbers between the observations. These predictions still require validation.
 
This is an illustrative example with synthetic data, not a validated drag correlation.


Classification
Classification predicts a category or discrete output from one or more features. For example, we may classify a flow as laminar or turbulent using its Reynolds number and angle of attack. Here, the two input quantities are the features, and the flow regime is the target. Each training example pairs specific Reynolds-number and angle-of-attack values with a class label, such as laminar or turbulent.
A classifier learns a rule for assigning a category to a feature combination. In the sketch below, a decision boundary separates the two predicted categories in feature space. The background shading shows the model prediction, while the marker shapes and colors show the observed class labels. Some observations lie in the region predicted for the other class, illustrating that the model does not classify every sample correctly. Unlike regression, the target is a category rather than a continuous value, although a classifier may also estimate the probability of each category.
 
The points and boundary are schematic. Actual transition depends on the geometry, disturbances, and other flow conditions; the line is not a physical transition criterion.



Unsupervised learning
In unsupervised learning, we seek structure in a dataset without providing target values or class labels for the training examples. Two common tasks are dimensionality reduction and clustering.

Dimensionality reduction
Dimensionality reduction represents data using fewer variables while retaining the information relevant to the task. A suitable coordinate transformation can reveal that much of the variation occurs along only a few directions.
Consider two probes measuring the streamwise velocity at different locations. At each sampling time, the measured values \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) form one point in a two-dimensional dataset. Suppose the measurements roughly follow a linear trend: when one probe records a higher velocity, the other usually does too.
We can center the dataset by subtracting the mean probe values and rotate the coordinate system to align its first axis with the direction of greatest variance. The transformed coordinates \(U'_1\) and \(U'_2\) are the principal-component coordinates. We will define principal components precisely later in the course.
 
In the transformed coordinates, the variance along \(U'_2\) is small compared with that along \(U'_1\). We may therefore discard \(U'_2\) and describe each sample using only \(U'_1\). The crosses show this one-dimensional representation; the short connecting lines show the discarded component. We have reduced the number of describing variables from two to one, with a small loss of information in this example.
The rotation itself does not discard information; the reduction occurs when we omit the second coordinate. Whether its small variance makes it safe to discard depends on the task: even a small fluctuation can be physically important. However, fluctuations may also arise from experimental measurement noise. If the discarded component mainly represents such noise, removing it can improve the data quality.


Clustering
Clustering groups samples according to their similarity without requiring predefined class labels. We choose how to represent each sample and how to measure similarity; a clustering method then seeks groups within that representation.
For example, suppose a flow repeatedly visits different states. We record two streamwise velocity probes and represent each sampling time by the pair \((U_1,U_2)\). Clustering these pairs can identify groups of similar probe readings. We can then inspect the corresponding flow snapshots to determine whether the groups represent recurring flow states, such as different wake configurations.
 
Each circular marker represents one sampling time. The crosses mark the cluster centers, and the enclosing circles indicate the groups of samples. These circles illustrate group membership rather than a learned decision boundary; the groups are not labels supplied before learning. Grouping snapshots can help us select representative states for closer analysis or build a reduced description of the flow.
A cluster does not automatically correspond to a distinct physical regime. Its interpretation depends on the chosen variables, their scaling, the similarity measure, and the clustering method. Two probes may also miss differences elsewhere in the flow, so we must check the interpretation against the associated flow fields.



Reinforcement learning
Reinforcement learning learns how to choose actions through interaction with an environment, using rewards to evaluate their consequences. The agent chooses actions according to a policy. The environment responds to an action and returns the next state and a reward. The aim is to improve the policy to maximize the expected cumulative reward.

Example: drag reduction with a rotating cylinder
Consider a cylinder that can rotate about its axis while fluid flows past it. We want to reduce its drag coefficient by controlling its rotation speed. A few pressure measurements in the cylinder’s wake provide the state used by the controller.
 
We use uppercase letters \(S_n\), \(A_n\), and \(R_{n+1}\) for random variables, and lowercase letters \(s_n\), \(a_n\), and \(r_{n+1}\) for their realized values. Accordingly, \(\pi(a\mid s)\) denotes the policy distribution evaluated at an action value \(a\) and a state value \(s\), while \(p(s'\mid s,a)\) describes the transition distribution for state values and an action value.
Strictly, we can distinguish the full physical state of the flow from the observations available to the controller. We will not make this distinction in this lecture: here, we use state for the pressure measurements supplied to the controller.

The agent is the controller that selects the cylinder’s rotation speed. The action random variable \(A_n\) represents the angular velocity imposed at step \(n\); a realized action is \(a_n=\omega_n\).
The state random variable \(S_n\) is a vector of pressure values measured at a few locations in the cylinder’s wake.
The policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\) is the control law. It maps the pressure measurements to a probability distribution over rotation speeds, from which the controller selects an action.
The state transition is the flow’s response to the rotating cylinder. In a simulation, the flow solver advances the solution under the imposed rotation speed and produces the pressure measurements that form the next state.
The reward is based on the drag coefficient \(c_D\). The reward random variable is \(R_{n+1}\). For a realized drag coefficient, the reward value \(r_{n+1}=-c_{D,n+1}\) assigns a higher reward when the drag coefficient is lower. Maximizing cumulative reward then encourages drag reduction over successive control steps.
During policy improvement, the learning algorithm uses collected pressure measurements, rotation speeds, and rewards to update the control law. Interaction supplies experience from which the controller can improve.

The reward expresses our chosen objective; it is not an intrinsic goal of the fluid. A practical control problem also specifies the allowed rotation speeds and may include the cost of rotating the cylinder in its objective.



Combining learning categories to solve real-world problems
Real-world problems often require several of the learning categories introduced above. A central challenge is to decompose a complex problem into subproblems that suitable methods can address.

Example: detecting anomalies in images of a process
Suppose we take images of an experimental or industrial process and want to detect when something goes wrong in the process chain. If we have examples labeled as normal or anomalous, we can pose this as a classification task. However, we may not want to classify the images directly in their full pixel space.
We can first use dimensionality reduction to obtain a compact representation of each image. The resulting coordinates are often called latent variables. A classifier then uses these variables to predict whether the process is behaving normally or showing an anomaly. This combines dimensionality reduction with classification.
If labeled anomalies are unavailable, we may instead learn a representation of normal behavior and detect departures from it. Anomaly detection therefore does not always require supervised classification. In either approach, the representation must retain the information that makes an anomaly detectable.


Example: reduced-order models of flows
A reduced-order flow model often combines dimensionality reduction with regression. First, we represent flow snapshots using a small number of latent variables. We can then fit a regression model that maps physical parameters to these variables, producing a parametric model. Alternatively, we can fit a model that predicts their future values from their current values or recent history, producing a model of the flow dynamics.
When needed, we reconstruct an approximate flow field from the predicted latent variables. The reduced representation and the predictive model work together: the first makes the problem smaller, while the second describes how the reduced variables depend on parameters or evolve over time.


Choosing methods for each subproblem
A workflow can combine more than two techniques, and not every subproblem requires machine learning. Classical numerical methods and analytical models can be combined with learned representations or predictors. For example, after reducing the dimensionality of a flow dataset, we might derive a simple analytical relationship in the latent coordinates and fit its remaining parameters to data, rather than train a more flexible learned predictor.
The important task is to identify which parts of the problem involve prediction, grouping, representation, or control, and then choose methods that suit each part. We must also check how the parts interact: information discarded in one step may be essential to a later step, and errors can propagate through the workflow.

title: Course overview and motivation
text:
Challenges encountered in machine learning
Machine learning can help us analyze data and build models, but a successful fit does not by itself establish that a model is useful or reliable. Several challenges arise throughout the workflow.

Obtaining suitable data
The data must contain information relevant to the question we want to answer. Measurements may contain noise, missing values, or systematic errors. Simulation data depend on the physical models, numerical resolution, boundary conditions, and convergence of the calculation. A model can learn these errors along with the relationships we intended it to learn.
Coverage matters too. A dataset collected at one Reynolds number or for one geometry may not support predictions under different conditions. More data are helpful when they add relevant information; collecting many nearly identical snapshots does not necessarily improve coverage.


Generalizing beyond the training examples
A model may reproduce its training data accurately but perform poorly on unseen examples. This is called overfitting. We therefore need validation and test data that reflect the intended application and are kept separate from model fitting.
In fluid mechanics, nearby snapshots from the same trajectory can be strongly correlated. Randomly distributing these snapshots across training and test sets may give an overly optimistic impression of performance. Depending on the task, a more meaningful check may hold out entire simulations, operating conditions, or time intervals. Preprocessing, including scaling and dimensionality reduction, must also be fitted using only the training data to avoid leaking information from the test set.
Interpolation and extrapolation pose different challenges. Good predictions within the sampled range do not establish that a model will remain reliable at unseen Reynolds numbers, geometries, or flow regimes.


Fitting and choosing models
Learning often requires optimizing many parameters. The optimization problem may be nonlinear or nonconvex, and its outcome can depend on initialization, variable scaling, and training settings. Model complexity must be appropriate for the available data and the task: a model that is too simple may miss relevant relationships, while an overly flexible model may fit noise.
We must also choose how to measure success. A small average prediction error can conceal large errors in rare but important events. For anomaly detection, for example, classifying every image as normal may appear accurate when anomalies are rare, while failing at the actual task.


Managing computational cost
Large flow datasets can exceed available memory or make repeated training and analysis expensive. Efficient data structures, selective storage, processing in batches, and parallel algorithms can help. The complete workflow matters: reading and transforming data may cost as much as fitting the model.
A learned model should also be evaluated under its intended operating conditions. A controller must produce actions quickly enough, and a model embedded in a flow solver must remain affordable when evaluated repeatedly.


Establishing physical reliability
A statistically accurate prediction need not satisfy conservation laws, boundary conditions, or other physical constraints. We need checks that are meaningful for the application, including simple cases, limiting behavior, and comparisons with independent data or methods.
Errors can also accumulate when a model predicts a trajectory over many time steps or interacts with a simulation or control loop. Evaluating isolated predictions is therefore insufficient for these applications; we must test the resulting dynamics and report where the model is reliable and what remains uncertain.

title: Course overview and motivation
section: How to combine machine learning and fluid mechanics
text:
How to combine machine learning and fluid mechanics
Experiments and CFD simulations can both produce data and use models learned from data. The following workflows describe four common ways to connect them. The operations on the arrows are extract, learn, and use.

Extract data and learn models
We extract data from a CFD simulation or an experiment and learn models from those data. The models can provide predictions or representations that help us understand the flow.
 
Examples include surrogate modeling, where a model predicts quantities such as forces from operating conditions, and flow analysis, where a learned representation helps identify coherent structures or recurring flow states.


Learn models and use them in CFD or experiments
We start with available data, learn models, and use those models in a CFD simulation or an experiment.
 
For example, experimental velocity measurements can provide data for a model of an inlet profile or its time dependence. We can then use this model as a more realistic boundary condition in a CFD simulation.
Other examples include material models, such as a relationship between temperature and viscosity, and closure models for turbulence or multiphase flow. In an experiment, a learned model may help prescribe operating conditions or settings based on measured data.


Combine workflows across scales or levels of complexity
The first two workflows can be combined and repeated. A CFD simulation or experiment of type 1 provides data from which we learn models. We then use those models in a simulation or experiment of type 2, extract new data, and continue the process.
 
This is useful for modeling approaches that reduce the resolved range of scales or the complexity of the description. We first investigate small-scale phenomena in detail, then compress their behavior into models. A second investigation uses these models to account for small-scale effects without resolving all their details.
For example, a detailed investigation of mass transfer around individual bubbles can supply a closure model for a larger-scale multiphase-flow simulation. Further stages may replace individual bubbles with an averaged description of the mixture.


Close the loop
In a circular workflow, we extract data from a CFD simulation or an experiment, learn models, and use those models in the same system. Their use changes the system’s behavior, generating new data for the next learning step.
 
Examples include active flow control and parameter optimization. In rotating-cylinder control, pressure measurements and drag coefficients provide data for improving a policy. Applying the updated policy changes the cylinder’s rotation and the resulting flow, which produces new data. In parameter optimization, a learned model can guide the choice of the next operating parameters to evaluate.
